zh.q: 桌上是些什么？电流从哪来、往哪走？
zh.concl: 光一照，阴极 K 就发射光电子、阳极 A 把它们收走，电路里形成光电流；U = 0 时电流也不为 0（电子本来就有初动能）；这个电流的产生几乎是瞬时的——教材只说「立即 / 几乎是瞬时发生的」，没有给数量级，所以本课也不显示任何建立时间。
points: 光电管里 K 在右、A 在左，光从管顶窗口射到 K 上（照图4.2-1 原图，不能画反）。
μA 表串在阴极 K 支路，电压表并在管两端；分压器给出 0…6.00 V，换向开关决定正负。
光一照就有电流、一遮就没有（中控台的「遮光板」开关），本课不显示任何建立时间。

zh.q: 电压一格一格加上去，电流会一直变大吗？
zh.concl: 教材 p.72：随电压增大光电流趋于饱和值，再增大电压也不增大——因为单位时间逃出的电子数一定，电压够大时全被 A 收走；U = 0 时电流不为 0。
points: U = 0 时电流不为 0（0.294 μA）——电子逸出时本来就带着初动能。
饱和电流由光强定，不由电压定；I_sat 格要加到 6.00 V 才亮，且比真值小 0.0069 μA（方向可复算）。
曲线在正向段的形状是课件示意（教材只有图4.2-2 的示意曲线）；「趋于饱和」「U = 0 时电流不为 0」这两句是教材原话，曲线怎么升不是。

zh.q: 把电源对调，电流会怎样？加到哪里电流恰好没有？
zh.concl: 教材 p.72：使光电流减小到 0 的反向电压叫遏止电压 Uc，且 ½mₑv_c² = eU_c。教材只给「使光电流减小到 0 的反向电压」这个定义；「−Uc 到 0 之间逐渐降到 0」是本课按原句（vc 是最大速度）推出来的一句，不是教材原话。
points: Uc 的定义是「使光电流减小到 0」的反向电压——只看「变小」会把 Uc 测小（A4.4、A7.8）。
读数格只在你停在那一格时出现：−1.10 V（0.002）是「—」、−1.11 V（第一次归零）才亮 1.11、−1.12 V（上一格已是 0）又回「—」。
Uc ≥ 0 只是大小；反向时 U = −Uc 是负的（A7.7）。

zh.q: 同一个颜色、光更强，电流和遏止电压各怎么变？
zh.concl: 教材 p.72：频率不变时入射光越强，饱和电流越大（光子数多 → 电子数多）；无论光的强弱如何，遏止电压都是一样的——光强只改电子个数，不改每个电子的能量。
points: Uc 与光强无关（两条黄光都是 0.03 V；钠 365 的三档也都是 1.11 V，断言 D4「差 = 0.00 V」）。
4.640 μA 已到量程的 92.8 %，光强再大就顶表、饱和电流就测小（B1.1）——保留这一档，正是要看见这条提示。

zh.q: 换一片滤光片，遏止电压会变吗？频率太低会怎样？
zh.concl: 教材 p.72：光的频率改变时 Uc 也会改变；频率减小到某一数值 νc 时光电流消失，低于截止频率就不发生光电效应（与光强、与电压都无关）。
points: 截止频率由金属自己定：钠 546.1 nm（5.4935 < 5.53）一个电子都没有，怎么扫都扫不到零点。
低于 νc 时光再强也没用（三档光强、三个电压全是 0.000，断言 D3）。

zh.q: 同一束光换一种阴极，为什么一个电子都没有？
zh.concl: 教材 p.73 表 + p.72：截止频率与金属自身的性质有关（νc = W₀/h）。所以同一束光，换一种阴极就可能一只光电子都没有；同一频率下 W₀ 越大的金属 Uc 越小。
points: 截止频率是金属自己的性质（钠 5.53 / 钾 5.44 / 铷 5.15×10¹⁴ Hz，教材 p.73 表）。
同一频率下 W₀ 越大 Uc 越小（1.11 < 1.15 < 1.27）。
三种阴极的饱和电流相同（P 200 时都 2.935 μA）只因为本课把量子效率取成同一个值——这是课件设定（示意），教材没有这个结论。

zh.q: 把每个频率和它对应的 Uc 画在图上，会得到什么？
zh.concl: 教材 p.75：U_c = (h/e)ν − W₀/e，Uc-ν 是一条斜率为 h/e 的直线 → h = e·斜率。这正是教材 p.77 练习第 4 题的做法：同一只管子、两条以上频率已知的光。图4.2-5 只借「点 + 红直线」的形态：图题只说「某金属」，其斜率比 h/e 小约 5 %，所以图上的点值本课不取。
points: 斜率只由 h/e 决定，换金属只改截距与横轴截距 νc（A7.11、A7.12）。
h_测 差 −0.46 %，落在教材说的 0.5 % 量级内（A2.11、D6）。
记录行只记停在零点那一格的 Uc（addRow 在 Uc 是「—」时拒收）；Uc 只有两三格的谱线不能拿进拟合。

zh.q: 铭牌写着 2.29 eV，为什么测出来对不上？
zh.concl: 两件事分开说：① 标称 ≠ 实际——教材 p.73 表里的 2.29 eV 是「钠这种金属」的值；这只管子的阴极表面状态不同，实际 W₀ = 2.305 eV，所以同一频率下 Uc 小 0.015 V。这才是「必须测、不能只看表」的理由。② 两处测量误差各有方向、要分开算再合：分度 0.01 V 让 Uc_测 只能落在格点上、向上取（理想档 +0.0008 V，恒在 0～+0.01 V）；真实档电压刻度 +0.4 % 让实际电压比读数大，零点落到更小的读数上（真值折成读数 1.0898 V，读数偏小 0.0044 V）；两处一起 = 测得 1.09 V，比真值 1.0942 小 0.0042 V——所以 1.09 < 1.0942 不是算错。此外 I_sat_测 因 6.00 V 未到 100 % 而偏小 0.0069 μA；光强超量程时读数削平在 5.000 → 饱和电流一定测小（Uc 不受影响）。
points: 真实档三处偏差是固定常数，同一个工况永远同一组读数（确定性，不是随机误差）。
两处误差方向相反、要分开算再合：分度让 Uc_测 偏大 0～+0.01 V（这次 +0.0008），刻度 +0.4 % 让它偏小 0.0044 V，合起来 1.09 V。
超量程只让 I_sat 测小、Uc 不受影响（反向段电流只有 0.1–0.6 μA）。

zh.q: 考核：给一只没标定的真实管子，你该选哪条谱线、多强、加到多少，才算测出了一个合格的 Uc？
zh.concl: 没有新结论：ν > νc 才有电子、反向要加到读数恰为 0.000 且是第一次归零才是 Uc、Uc 太小（< 0.10 V）时两三格测不准、光强不能大到让这一档的饱和电流超量程——四条全在前面几步里；W₀ = hν/e − Uc 就是第 7 步那条直线在同一只管子上的单点用法。
points: 先判断这束光能不能激发这只管子（ν vs νc），再谈测量。
反向必须扫到读数恰为 0.000 且是第一次归零；停在 0.002 会把 Uc 测小一格，停在过了零点的格子上则拿不到读数。
Uc 只有两三格（< 0.10 V）的工况测不准；光强要选到让这一档的饱和电流 ≤ 4.000 μA（量程 80 %）。

en.q: What is on the bench? Where does the current come from and where does it go?
en.concl: When light shines, cathode K emits photoelectrons and anode A collects them, so a photocurrent flows in the circuit; even at U = 0 the current is not zero (the electrons already have kinetic energy); the current appears almost instantly. The textbook only says "immediately / almost instantaneously" and gives no order of magnitude, so this lesson shows no build-up time.
points: In the phototube K is on the right and A on the left; light enters through the window at the top of the tube and falls on K (as in Fig. 4.2-1; do not draw it the other way round).
The μA meter is in series in the cathode K branch and the voltmeter is across the tube; the divider gives 0…6.00 V and the reversing switch sets the sign.
Light on means current, light blocked means none (the "shutter" switch on the console); this lesson shows no build-up time.

en.q: Raise the voltage step by step: does the current keep growing?
en.concl: Textbook p. 72: as the voltage rises the photocurrent approaches a saturation value and rises no further, because the number of electrons escaping per unit time is fixed, and a large enough voltage collects them all at A; at U = 0 the current is not zero.
points: At U = 0 the current is not zero (0.294 μA): electrons already carry kinetic energy when they escape.
The saturation current is set by light intensity, not by voltage; the I_sat box only lights up at 6.00 V, and reads 0.0069 μA below the true value (you can work out the direction).

The shape of the forward part of the curve is illustrative (the textbook only has the sketch in Fig. 4.2-2); "approaches saturation" and "the current is not zero at U = 0" are the textbook's words, how the curve rises is not.

en.q: Swap the supply: what happens to the current? At what voltage does it just stop?
en.concl: Textbook p. 72: the reverse voltage that brings the photocurrent down to 0 is the stopping voltage Uc, and ½mₑv_c² = eU_c. The textbook only defines it as "the reverse voltage that brings the photocurrent down to 0"; "falls gradually to 0 between −Uc and 0" is this lesson's inference from that sentence (vc is the maximum speed), not the textbook's words.
points: Uc is defined as the reverse voltage that "brings the photocurrent down to 0"; watching only for "smaller" makes you measure Uc too low (A4.4, A7.8).
The reading box only appears while you stay on that step: −1.10 V (0.002) shows "—", −1.11 V (first zero) lights up 1.11, and −1.12 V (previous step already 0) goes back to "—".
Uc ≥ 0 is only a magnitude; in reverse U = −Uc is negative (A7.7).

en.q: Same color, brighter light: how do the current and the stopping voltage change?
en.concl: Textbook p. 72: at a fixed frequency, the brighter the light, the larger the saturation current (more photons → more electrons); whatever the intensity, the stopping voltage is the same. Intensity only changes how many electrons there are, not the energy of each one.
points: At a fixed frequency I_sat ∝ intensity (4.640 : 2.320 = 2.000).
Uc does not depend on intensity (both yellow curves give 0.03 V; all three intensities of sodium at 365 give 1.11 V, check D4 "difference = 0.00 V").
4.640 μA is already 92.8 % of the range; any brighter and the meter maxes out and the saturation current reads low (B1.1). This setting is kept precisely so you see the warning.

en.q: Swap the filter: does the stopping voltage change? What if the frequency is too low?
en.concl: Textbook p. 72: when the frequency of the light changes, Uc changes too; when the frequency falls to a certain value νc the photocurrent disappears, and below the cutoff frequency there is no photoelectric effect (whatever the intensity or voltage).
points: Uc rises steadily with ν (sodium: 0.56 → 0.78 → 1.11, successive differences −0.22 / −0.33 V).
The cutoff frequency is set by the metal itself: sodium at 546.1 nm (5.4935 < 5.53) gives not a single electron, however you scan.
Below νc brighter light does not help (three intensities, three voltages, all 0.000; check D3).

en.q: Same light, different cathode: why are there no electrons at all?
en.concl: Textbook table p. 73 + p. 72: the cutoff frequency depends on the metal itself (νc = W₀/h). So the same light may produce no photoelectrons at all from a different cathode, and at the same frequency the metal with the larger W₀ has the smaller Uc.
points: The cutoff frequency is a property of the metal (sodium 5.53 / potassium 5.44 / rubidium 5.15×10¹⁴ Hz, textbook table p. 73).
At the same frequency, the larger W₀, the smaller Uc (1.11 < 1.15 < 1.27).

The three cathodes have the same saturation current (2.935 μA at P 200) only because this lesson gives them the same quantum efficiency; that is a lesson setting (illustrative), not a textbook result.

en.q: Plot each frequency against its Uc: what do you get?
en.concl: Textbook p. 75: U_c = (h/e)ν − W₀/e, so Uc vs ν is a straight line of slope h/e → h = e × slope. This is exactly the method of textbook p. 77 exercise 4: the same tube, two or more lights of known frequency. Only the "points + red line" look is borrowed from Fig. 4.2-5: its caption just says "a certain metal" and its slope is about 5 % below h/e, so this lesson does not use its values.
points: The slope depends only on h/e; changing the metal only changes the intercept and the frequency-axis intercept νc (A7.11, A7.12).
h_measured is −0.46 % off, within the 0.5 % the textbook mentions (A2.11, D6).
A record row only takes the Uc of the step stopped at zero (addRow refuses when Uc shows "—"); spectral lines whose Uc is only two or three steps cannot go into the fit.

en.q: The plate says 2.29 eV: why doesn't the measurement match?
en.concl: Two separate points. ① Nominal ≠ actual: the 2.29 eV in the textbook table on p. 73 is the value for "sodium as a metal"; the surface of this tube's cathode is different, its actual W₀ is 2.305 eV, so at the same frequency Uc is 0.015 V lower. That is why you must measure and not just look up the table. ② The two measurement errors each have a direction and must be worked out separately before combining: the 0.01 V step means Uc_measured can only land on a step and rounds up (ideal setting +0.0008 V, always within 0 to +0.01 V); in the real setting the voltage scale reads +0.4 %, so the actual voltage is higher than the reading and the zero falls on a smaller reading (the true value converts to a reading of 1.0898 V, 0.0044 V low); together they give 1.09 V measured, 0.0042 V below the true 1.0942, so 1.09 < 1.0942 is not a calculation mistake. In addition I_sat_measured is 0.0069 μA low because 6.00 V is not quite 100 %; when the intensity exceeds the range the reading is clipped at 5.000, so the saturation current is always measured low (Uc is not affected).
points: The three deviations in the real setting are fixed constants: the same conditions always give the same readings (deterministic, not random error).

The two errors point in opposite directions and must be worked out separately before combining: the step size makes Uc_measured 0 to +0.01 V high (+0.0008 this time), the +0.4 % scale makes it 0.0044 V low, together 1.09 V.
Exceeding the range only makes I_sat read low; Uc is not affected (the reverse current is only 0.1–0.6 μA).

en.q: Assessment: given an uncalibrated real tube, which spectral line, what intensity and how much voltage do you need to measure a valid Uc?
en.concl: No new conclusion: electrons appear only for ν > νc; Uc is the reverse voltage where the reading is exactly 0.000 for the first time; when Uc is too small (< 0.10 V) two or three steps cannot measure it accurately; the intensity must not be so high that the saturation current at that setting exceeds the range. All four came up in earlier steps; W₀ = hν/e − Uc is the single-point use of the step 7 line on the same tube.
points: First decide whether this light can excite this tube (ν vs νc), then measure.
The reverse scan must reach a reading of exactly 0.000 for the first time; stopping at 0.002 measures Uc one step low, and stopping past the zero gives no reading.
Conditions where Uc is only two or three steps (< 0.10 V) cannot be measured accurately; choose an intensity whose saturation current is ≤ 4.000 μA (80 % of the range).
